VSA-001.q: The current set of 37 Vietnamese Standards on Auditing was issued under:
VSA-001.e: Circular 214/2012/TT-BTC of 06/12/2012 issued 37 standards (VSQC1 and 36 VSAs).
VSA-001.x:
Basis: Circular 214/2012/TT-BTC of 06/12/2012.
Analysis: Circular 214/2012 issued 37 standards: 1 quality control standard (VSQC1) and 36 auditing standards (VSA 200–810), modelled on IAASB's ISAs.
Distractors: Circular 200/2014 is the corporate accounting regime; Circular 70/2015 is the ethics code; Decision 345/QĐ-BTC is the IFRS roadmap.

VSA-002.q: The 37 auditing standards under Circular 214/2012/TT-BTC took effect from:
VSA-002.e: They apply to financial statement audits from 2014.
VSA-002.x:
Basis: Circular 214/2012/TT-BTC (effective-date clause).
Analysis: Effective from 01/01/2014, applying to FS audits from 2014 – giving audit firms about a year to prepare.
Distractors: B is the issue date; C and D are wrong.

VSA-003.x:
Basis: Circular 214/2012/TT-BTC.
Analysis: True. It was signed on 06/12/2012, effective 01/01/2014 (VSA-002).
Note: Distinguish issue and effective dates – a common trap in quiz questions.

VSA-004.e: VSQM1: quality management at audit firms; VSQM2: engagement quality reviews.
o: Quality management standards VSQM1 and VSQM2
VSA-004.x:
Basis: Circular 137/2026/TT-BTC of 24/09/2026 (per the question's source); IAASB ISQM 1 and ISQM 2.
Analysis: It issues VSQM1 – Quality management for audit firms (equivalent to ISQM 1) and VSQM2 – Engagement quality reviews (equivalent to ISQM 2).
Distractors: B is still a draft (VSA-007); C is Circular 70/2015; D is Circular 99/2025.
Note: This post-dates the assistant's knowledge; check the original.

VSA-005.q: VSQM1 and VSQM2 under Circular 137/2026/TT-BTC take effect from:
VSA-005.e: A long transition lets audit firms design their quality management systems.
VSA-005.x:
Basis: Circular 137/2026/TT-BTC (per the question's source).
Analysis: VSQM1 and VSQM2 take effect on 01/01/2029 – over two years for firms to design risk-based quality management (objectives, risks, responses).
Distractors: C is the issue date; B and D are wrong.
Note: Internationally, ISQM 1 took effect on 15/12/2022.

VSA-006.q: The quality control standard VSQC1 ceases to apply from 01/01/2029, when VSQM1 takes effect.
VSA-006.x:
Basis: Circular 137/2026/TT-BTC (per the question's source).
Analysis: True. VSQM1 replaces VSQC1 (Circular 214/2012), which lapses from 01/01/2029. Until then firms still apply VSQC1.

VSA-007.q: As of 19/10/2026, the MOF has officially issued a circular replacing 31 Vietnamese Standards on Auditing.
VSA-007.e: False. The update of 31 VSAs is still at the draft circular consultation stage.
VSA-007.x:
Basis: Draft circular issuing 31 VSAs (2026) (per the question's source).
Analysis: False. As of 19/10/2026, updating 31 VSAs to the revised ISAs was still at the consultation-draft stage; the 37 standards under Circular 214/2012 remain in force.
Note: Status may change after that date; check the Ministry of Finance portal.

VSA-008.q: Select ALL standards in the 2026 draft list of 31 updated VSAs:
VSA-008.e: The draft excludes VSA 501, 505, 520, 530, 600, 620; VSA 701 is new.
o: VSA 315 – Identifying and assessing the risks of material misstatement
VSA 501 – Audit evidence – specific considerations for selected items
VSA-008.x:
Basis: Draft circular issuing 31 VSAs (2026) (per the question's source).
Analysis: In the draft: (A) VSA 701 – key audit matters (new); (B) VSA 315 – risk assessment (per revised ISA 315, 2019); (C) VSA 540 – accounting estimates (per revised ISA 540, 2018).
Distractors: (D) The draft excludes VSA 501, 505, 520, 530, 600 and 620 per the question's source.
Note: The draft post-dates the assistant's knowledge.

VSA-009.q: VSA 701 on key audit matters (KAM) is not among the 37 standards issued under Circular 214/2012/TT-BTC.
VSA-009.e: True. KAM is introduced in the draft update, following IAASB's ISA 701.
VSA-009.x:
Basis: Circular 214/2012/TT-BTC; ISA 701 (IAASB, internationally effective for periods ending on or after 15/12/2016).
Analysis: True. The 2012 standards predate ISA 701 (issued 2015), so there's no VSA 701. KAMs – the most significant matters in the auditor's judgment, shown in the audit report (mainly for listed entities) – are added in the update draft.

VSA-010.q: The current Law on Independent Audit is:
VSA-010.e: Law 88/2015 is the Accounting Law; 81/2015 is the State Audit Law.
VSA-010.x:
Basis: Independent Audit Law 67/2011/QH12; Law 56/2024/QH15.
Analysis: The Independent Audit Law 67/2011/QH12 (effective 01/01/2012), amended by Law 56/2024/QH15.
Distractors: B – Accounting Law 88/2015; C – State Audit Law 81/2015; D – Enterprise Law 59/2020.

VSA-011.q: Law 56/2024/QH15 amended the Law on Independent Audit.
VSA-011.e: True. Law 56/2024/QH15 amended several finance laws, including the Accounting Law and the Independent Audit Law.
VSA-011.x:
Basis: Law 56/2024/QH15.
Analysis: True. Law 56/2024/QH15 amends several finance laws, including the Securities, Accounting and Independent Audit Laws (effective 01/01/2025 – ACC-086), including rules on auditing public-interest entities.

VSA-012.q: The decree detailing the Law on Independent Audit is:
VSA-012.e: Decree 05/2019 covers internal audit; Decree 174/2016 guides the Accounting Law.
VSA-012.x:
Basis: Decree 17/2012/ND-CP; Decree 90/2025/ND-CP (per the question's source).
Analysis: Decree 17/2012/ND-CP details the Independent Audit Law (mandatory audits, licensing conditions), amended by Decree 90/2025/ND-CP.
Distractors: B – internal audit; C – Accounting Law guidance; D – Securities Law guidance.
Note: Decree 90/2025 is cited per the question's source; check the original.

VSA-013.q: The current Vietnamese code of ethics for accountants and auditors was issued under:
VSA-013.e: Circular 70/2015/TT-BTC is based on the IESBA Code.
VSA-013.x:
Basis: Circular 70/2015/TT-BTC.
Analysis: Circular 70/2015/TT-BTC issues the professional ethics standard for accounting and auditing, based on the IESBA Code; it applies to auditors, accounting practitioners and accountants.
Distractors: B – auditing standards; C – accounting regime; D – provisions.

VSA-014.q: Select ALL entities subject to mandatory annual financial statement audit under the independent audit law:
VSA-014.e: Household businesses are not subject to mandatory audit.
VSA-014.x:
Basis: Article 37 of Independent Audit Law 67/2011/QH12; Article 15 of Decree 17/2012/ND-CP.
Analysis: Mandatory annual FS audits: (A) FDI enterprises; (B) credit institutions; (C) insurers; (D) public companies (plus State enterprises, financial institutions, national key projects…).
Distractors: (E) Household businesses aren't enterprises and aren't covered.

VSA-015.q: Match each auditing standard with its topic:
VSA-015.x:
Basis: Circular 214/2012/TT-BTC.
Analysis: VSA 230 – audit documentation; VSA 240 – responsibilities for fraud; VSA 570 – going concern; VSA 580 – written representations; VSA 705 – modified opinions.
Note: VSA numbers mirror ISAs: 200s – principles and responsibilities; 300–400s – risk assessment; 500s – evidence; 600s – using others' work; 700s – reporting.

VSA-016.q: Match each auditing standard with its topic:
VSA-016.e: The VSA 500 series covers audit evidence.
VSA-016.x:
Basis: Circular 214/2012/TT-BTC.
Analysis: VSA 500 – audit evidence; VSA 505 – external confirmations; VSA 520 – analytical procedures; VSA 530 – audit sampling; VSA 560 – subsequent events. The 500 series covers evidence.

VSA-017.q: Vietnamese Standards on Auditing are based on IAASB's International Standards on Auditing (ISA), adapted to Vietnam.
VSA-017.e: True. The 2026 draft updates VSAs to the revised ISAs.
VSA-017.x:
Basis: Circular 214/2012/TT-BTC.
Analysis: True. VSAs are based on IAASB's ISAs, adapted to Vietnamese law and conditions. Since ISAs keep changing (ISA 315 – 2019, ISA 540 – 2018, ISA 701 – 2015), the Ministry is updating VSAs via the 2026 draft (VSA-008).

VSA-018.q: The State Audit Office audits under its own state audit standards based on the State Audit Law, not under VSAs.
VSA-018.e: True. VSAs govern independent audits by audit firms.
VSA-018.x:
Basis: State Audit Law 81/2015/QH13.
Analysis: True. The State Audit Office audits public finances and assets under State auditing standards issued by the Auditor General. VSAs govern independent audits by audit firms.

VSA-019.q: Match each fundamental ethical principle with its content:
VSA-019.e: The five fundamental principles under Circular 70/2015/TT-BTC.
p: Straightforward and honest in all professional relationships
No bias or conflict of interest overriding judgement
Maintain knowledge and skill and act diligently
Do not disclose information without authority
Comply with laws and avoid discrediting the profession
VSA-019.x:
Basis: Circular 70/2015/TT-BTC (5 fundamental principles).
Analysis: Integrity – straightforward and honest; objectivity – no bias, conflict of interest or undue influence on judgment; professional competence and due care – keeping skills current and working diligently; confidentiality – no unauthorised disclosure; professional behaviour – complying with law and avoiding discrediting the profession.

VSA-020.q: Select ALL categories of threats to compliance with ethical principles:
VSA-020.e: The five categories: self-interest, self-review, advocacy, familiarity, intimidation.
VSA-020.x:
Basis: Circular 70/2015/TT-BTC (threats and safeguards framework).
Analysis: Five threats: (A) self-interest – financial interests, fees; (B) self-review – re-evaluating one's own work; (C) advocacy – promoting the client's position; (D) familiarity – long or close relationships; (E) intimidation – actual or perceived pressure.
Distractors: (F) 'Professionalisation' isn't a threat category.

VSA-021.q: An engagement partner auditing the same client for many consecutive years creates a:
VSA-021.e: A typical safeguard is partner rotation.
VSA-021.x:
Basis: Circular 70/2015/TT-BTC (key partner rotation).
Analysis: Leading the same client for years breeds closeness and acceptance of the client's views → familiarity threat. Typical safeguard: partner rotation (for public-interest entities, after a set number of years), plus independent review.
Distractors: B, C and D are other threats (VSA-020).

VSA-022.q: An audit firm that keeps the books and prepares a client's financial statements and also audits them creates a:
VSA-022.e: The auditor would be evaluating its own work.
VSA-022.x:
Basis: Circular 70/2015/TT-BTC; Independent Audit Law 67/2011/QH12 (limits on services to audit clients).
Analysis: Keeping books and preparing FS then auditing them is reviewing one's own work → self-review threat. For public-interest entities it's prohibited; for others only with safeguards and client ownership of management decisions.
Distractors: B, C and D are other threats.

VSA-023.q: Audit fees may be contingent on results (e.g., a % of audited profit).
VSA-023.e: False. Contingent fees for audit create an unacceptable self-interest threat.
VSA-023.x:
Basis: Circular 70/2015/TT-BTC (contingent fees).
Analysis: False. Outcome-based fees (e.g., a % of audited profit) give the auditor a stake in the very figures they attest – a self-interest threat no safeguard can reduce, so they're prohibited for audit and review engagements.

VSA-024.q: Audit team members may not hold a direct financial interest in the audit client.
VSA-024.e: True. A direct financial interest creates a severe self-interest threat to independence.
VSA-024.x:
Basis: Circular 70/2015/TT-BTC (financial interests); Independent Audit Law 67/2011/QH12.
Analysis: True. A direct financial interest (shares, capital) in an audit client creates a severe self-interest threat – the audit outcome affects the auditor's wealth. The only acceptable remedies are disposal or leaving the team; the rule extends to immediate family.

VSA-025.q: An auditor may disclose a client's confidential information when:
VSA-025.e: The duty of confidentiality continues after the relationship ends.
o: Required by law or permitted by the client
VSA-025.x:
Basis: Circular 70/2015/TT-BTC (confidentiality).
Analysis: Disclosure is allowed when required by law (authorities, legal proceedings), authorised by the client, or under professional duties and rights (Ministry or professional body quality reviews, defending one's interests in disputes).
Distractors: B and C have no basis; D is wrong – confidentiality continues after the relationship ends.

VSA-026.q: The correct distinction between VSQC1 and VSA 220 is:
VSA-026.e: The two standards complement each other in quality control.
o: VSQC1 applies at audit-firm level; VSA 220 at the level of each engagement
VSA-026.x:
Basis: VSQC1 and VSA 220 (Circular 214/2012/TT-BTC).
Analysis: VSQC1 applies at firm level – the firm-wide quality control system; VSA 220 applies at engagement level – duties of the engagement partner and team. They complement each other.
Distractors: B, C and D misstate their scope.

VSA-027.q: VSQM1 shifts from prescriptive quality control to risk-based quality management.
VSA-027.e: True. The firm sets quality objectives, identifies risks and designs responses.
VSA-027.x:
Basis: Circular 137/2026/TT-BTC – VSQM1 (per the question's source); ISQM 1.
Analysis: True. VSQC1 sets fixed requirements; VSQM1 (per ISQM 1) moves to risk-based quality management: firms set quality objectives, identify and assess quality risks and design responses suited to their size and nature, with ongoing monitoring and remediation.

VSA-028.q: Select ALL components of the quality management system under VSQM1:
VSA-028.e: The eight components also include relevant ethical requirements, engagement performance, resources, and information and communication.
o: Acceptance and continuance of client relationships and engagements
Fee policy based on client revenue
VSA-028.x:
Basis: VSQM1 (Circular 137/2026/TT-BTC, per the question's source); ISQM 1.
Analysis: Eight components: (A) the firm's risk assessment process; (B) governance and leadership; (C) acceptance and continuance of clients and engagements; (D) monitoring and remediation; plus relevant ethical requirements; engagement performance; resources; information and communication.
Distractors: (E) Pricing fees on client revenue isn't a component and may create a self-interest threat.

VSA-029.e: Engagement quality reviewers must have competence, authority and objectivity.
o: Engagement quality reviews: appointment, eligibility of reviewers and performing the review
VSA-029.x:
Basis: VSQM2 (Circular 137/2026/TT-BTC, per the question's source); ISQM 2.
Analysis: VSQM2 governs engagement quality reviews: appointing reviewers, eligibility (competence, authority, objectivity – including a cooling-off period before a former engagement partner can review), performing and documenting the review.
Distractors: B – VSA 300; C – VSA 700/705; D – Circular 70/2015.

VSA-030.q: Under VSA 220, the engagement partner is responsible for the overall quality of the audit.
VSA-030.e: True. This responsibility cannot be fully delegated.
VSA-030.x:
Basis: VSA 220 (Circular 214/2012/TT-BTC).
Analysis: True. The engagement partner is responsible for overall audit quality: direction, supervision, review, ethics and independence, and signing the report. Tasks may be delegated but responsibility can't be fully handed off.

VSA-031.q: Audits of listed entities' financial statements require an engagement quality control review before the report is issued.
VSA-031.e: True under VSQC1 and VSA 220; VSQM2 retains this requirement.
VSA-031.x:
Basis: VSQC1; VSA 220 (Circular 214/2012/TT-BTC); VSQM2.
Analysis: True. Audits of listed entities' FS (and other engagements the firm designates) require an independent engagement quality review before the report is issued – evaluating significant judgments and conclusions. VSQM2 keeps this requirement.

VSA-032.e: Skepticism means critical assessment, not doubting everything.
o: A questioning mind, alert to signs of misstatement due to error or fraud, and critical assessment of evidence
VSA-032.x:
Basis: VSA 200 (Circular 214/2012/TT-BTC).
Analysis: Professional skepticism is a questioning mind, alert to signs of error or fraud, with critical assessment of evidence (contradictions, document reliability).
Distractors: B assumes dishonesty – the opposite bias; C is impractical; D contradicts skepticism – representations don't replace evidence.

VSA-033.q: Significant professional judgements and their basis must be documented in the audit file.
VSA-033.e: True under VSA 230: the file must let an experienced auditor understand the work done.
VSA-033.x:
Basis: VSA 230 (Circular 214/2012/TT-BTC).
Analysis: True. Files must let an experienced auditor with no prior involvement understand: the nature, timing and extent of procedures; results and evidence; significant matters, conclusions and key judgments with their basis. In inspections, 'not documented = not done'.

VSA-034.q: When a threat to independence is identified, the auditor should:
VSA-034.e: This is the threats-and-safeguards conceptual framework.
o: Identify and evaluate the threat and apply safeguards; if it cannot be reduced to an acceptable level, decline or withdraw
Ignore it if the client agrees
Merely note it in the file
VSA-034.x:
Basis: Circular 70/2015/TT-BTC (threats and safeguards approach).
Analysis: Sequence: identify threats → evaluate significance → apply safeguards to eliminate or reduce them to an acceptable level; if impossible, decline or end the engagement.
Distractors: B – client consent doesn't remove threats; C – a note doesn't address them; D increases self-interest.

VSA-035.q: Arrange the process for accepting a new audit client:
VSA-035.e: Sign only after assessing client acceptance risk.
o: Understand the client and management's integrity
Communicate with the predecessor auditor (if any)
Agree terms and sign the engagement letter
VSA-035.x:
Basis: VSQC1; VSA 210; VSA 220; Circular 70/2015/TT-BTC (communicating with predecessors).
Analysis: Order: (1) understand the client and management integrity; (2) assess competence and resources; (3) assess independence and ethics; (4) contact the predecessor auditor (reasons for change, disagreements); (5) agree terms and sign. Sign only once acceptance risk is acceptable.

VSA-036.q: Consider these statements on VSA 210 – Audit engagement terms:
VSA-036.e: Preparing FS is management's responsibility; a written agreement is mandatory.
o: Engagement terms must be agreed in writing.
Management's acknowledgement of responsibility for preparing the FS is a precondition.
The auditor is responsible for preparing the entity's FS.
VSA-036.x:
Basis: VSA 210 – Agreeing the terms of audit engagements (Circular 214/2012/TT-BTC).
Analysis: True: terms must be agreed in writing (contract or engagement letter); management acknowledging responsibility for the FS, internal control and providing information is a precondition. False: preparing FS is management's duty, not the auditor's; a written engagement is mandatory.

VSA-037.e: The risk of material misstatement comprises inherent risk and control risk.
o: Risk of material misstatement × Detection risk
VSA-037.x:
Basis: VSA 200 (Circular 214/2012/TT-BTC).
Analysis: Audit risk = Risk of material misstatement (RMM) × Detection risk, where RMM comprises inherent and control risk (expanded form IR × CR × DR – ICR-054).
Distractors: B adds; C is meaningless; D mixes unrelated concepts.

VSA-038.q: Match each risk with its definition:
VSA-038.e: The auditor assesses the first two and designs procedures to control detection risk.
p: Susceptibility of an assertion to material misstatement before considering controls
Internal control fails to prevent or detect misstatement on a timely basis
The auditor's procedures fail to detect a material misstatement
VSA-038.x:
Basis: VSA 200 (Circular 214/2012/TT-BTC).
Analysis: Inherent risk – susceptibility of an assertion to material misstatement before controls (due to the item's nature: complex estimates, cash transactions); control risk – IC failing to prevent or detect and correct in time; detection risk – the auditor's procedures failing to find the misstatement.

VSA-039.q: Of the components of audit risk, the auditor can directly control only detection risk.
VSA-039.e: True. Inherent and control risks exist independently of the audit.
VSA-039.x:
Basis: VSA 200 (Circular 214/2012/TT-BTC).
Analysis: True. Inherent and control risk belong to the entity and exist independently of the audit – the auditor can only assess them. Detection risk depends on the nature, timing and extent of the auditor's procedures, so the auditor controls it directly (VSA-040).

VSA-040.q: When the risk of material misstatement is assessed as high, the auditor should:
VSA-040.e: Inverse relationship: the higher the RMM, the lower the acceptable detection risk.
o: Reduce detection risk: more substantive procedures, closer to period end, larger samples
VSA-040.x:
Basis: VSA 330 (Circular 214/2012/TT-BTC).
Analysis: For a fixed target audit risk, high RMM → lower acceptable detection risk → more persuasive substantive procedures (nature), closer to year-end (timing), larger samples (extent).
Distractors: B and C go the wrong way; D – representations can't replace evidence.

VSA-041.q: The auditor's overall objective in a financial statement audit is to obtain:
VSA-041.e: Reasonable assurance is high but not absolute, given inherent limitations of an audit.
o: Reasonable assurance that the FS as a whole are free from material misstatement due to fraud or error
VSA-041.x:
Basis: VSA 200 (Circular 214/2012/TT-BTC).
Analysis: Overall objective: reasonable assurance that the FS as a whole are free of material misstatement, whether due to fraud or error, enabling an opinion on whether they're prepared per the applicable framework, and reporting accordingly.
Distractors: B and C are impossible given inherent limitations (VSA-042); D isn't an FS audit objective.

VSA-042.q: Reasonable assurance in a financial statement audit is absolute assurance.
VSA-042.e: False. Audits have inherent limitations: sampling, judgement, collusive fraud.
VSA-042.x:
Basis: VSA 200 (Circular 214/2012/TT-BTC).
Analysis: False. Reasonable assurance is high but not absolute because of inherent limitations: sampling rather than testing everything; judgment-heavy estimates; persuasive rather than conclusive evidence; collusive fraud and forged documents being hard to detect; reasonable time and cost constraints.

VSA-043.q: Under VSA 300, audit planning has two main outputs:
VSA-043.e: The strategy sets scope, timing and direction; the plan details the nature, timing and extent of procedures.
o: The overall audit strategy and the audit plan
The management letter and audit report
VSA-043.x:
Basis: VSA 300 – Planning (Circular 214/2012/TT-BTC).
Analysis: Two outputs: the overall audit strategy – scope, timing, direction, resources; the audit plan – detailed nature, timing and extent of risk assessment and further procedures. Both are updated as circumstances change.
Distractors: B are end-of-audit outputs; C and D aren't planning outputs.

VSA-044.q: For a profit-oriented entity with stable earnings, the benchmark usually used for overall materiality is:
VSA-044.e: When profit is volatile or near break-even, revenue, total assets or equity may be used.
o: Profit before tax from continuing operations
VSA-044.x:
Basis: VSA 320 – Materiality in planning and performing an audit.
Analysis: For profit-oriented entities with stable earnings, the usual benchmark is profit before tax from continuing operations – what users care about most. With volatile, break-even or loss results: revenue, total assets, equity or average profit.
Distractors: B, C and D don't reflect FS users' focus.

VSA-045.q: Profit before tax is VND 20 billion; the firm sets overall materiality at 5% of PBT. What is overall materiality (VND million)?
VSA-045.x:
Basis: VSA 320.
Working: Overall materiality = 20,000 × 5% = 1,000 million VND.
Note: 5% of PBT is common practice (often 3–10% depending on risk); VSAs set no fixed rate – it's a documented professional judgment.

VSA-046.q: Overall materiality is VND 1,000 million; performance materiality is 75%. What is performance materiality (VND million)?
VSA-046.x:
Basis: VSA 320 (performance materiality).
Working: Performance materiality = 1,000 × 75% = 750 million VND.
Note: Usually 50–75% of overall materiality; higher risk or many prior-year errors → a lower rate (50–60%) for a bigger buffer against undetected errors (VSA-048).

VSA-047.q: Overall materiality is VND 1,000 million; the firm's clearly trivial threshold is 5% of overall materiality. What is the threshold (VND million)?
VSA-047.e: 1,000 × 5% = 50 million VND; misstatements below it need not be accumulated.
VSA-047.x:
Basis: VSA 450 – Evaluation of misstatements identified during the audit.
Working: Clearly trivial threshold = 1,000 × 5% = 50 million VND. Misstatements below it are clearly trivial and needn't be accumulated.
Note: Practice is 3–5% of overall materiality; sub-threshold items suggesting fraud still need qualitative consideration.

VSA-048.q: Performance materiality is set below overall materiality to reduce the probability that aggregate uncorrected and undetected misstatements exceed overall materiality.
VSA-048.e: True. That is the purpose of performance materiality under VSA 320.
VSA-048.x:
Basis: VSA 320.
Analysis: True. Performance materiality is set below overall materiality to reduce to an appropriately low level the probability that uncorrected plus undetected misstatements exceed overall materiality – since many individually immaterial errors can add up to a material one.

VSA-049.q: Materiality should be revised during the audit if the auditor becomes aware of information that would have led to a different amount initially.
VSA-049.e: True. E.g., actual profit differs greatly from the figure used at planning.
VSA-049.x:
Basis: VSA 320 (revising materiality during the audit).
Analysis: True. If the auditor learns information that would have led to a different materiality initially (e.g., actual profit far below plan), materiality must be revised and further procedures reconsidered.

VSA-050.q: For a significant risk, the auditor must:
VSA-050.e: For significant risks, substantive analytical procedures alone are insufficient.
o: Perform substantive procedures specifically responsive to it; if relying on controls, test them in the current period
Ignore it if audited last year
VSA-050.x:
Basis: VSA 330; VSA 315 (significant risks).
Analysis: For significant risks, the auditor must perform substantive procedures specifically responsive to them; if only substantive procedures are used, they must include tests of details (not just analytics). If relying on controls, those controls must be tested in the current period – no reliance on prior-year evidence.
Distractors: B isn't enough; C and D breach the standard.

VSA-051.q: Under VSA 240, the auditor presumes a fraud risk in revenue recognition; the presumption may be rebutted with reasons documented in the file.
VSA-051.e: True. E.g., an entity with a single simple rental revenue stream.
VSA-051.x:
Basis: VSA 240 (Circular 214/2012/TT-BTC).
Analysis: True. Auditors presume a fraud risk in revenue recognition (revenue is easily managed to meet expectations). The presumption can be rebutted with reasons (e.g., one simple, fixed rental stream), which must be documented.

VSA-052.q: The risk of management override of controls exists in every entity and is a significant risk in every audit.
VSA-052.e: True. This presumption cannot be rebutted.
VSA-052.x:
Basis: VSA 240.
Analysis: True. Management is uniquely positioned to manipulate records and produce fraudulent FS by overriding controls that otherwise seem effective. The level varies, but the risk exists in every entity, is significant and can't be rebutted (unlike the revenue presumption, VSA-051).

VSA-053.q: Select ALL mandatory procedures responding to the risk of management override:
VSA-053.e: Confirming all customers is not required under VSA 240.
o: Test the appropriateness of journal entries and adjustments in preparing the FS
Evaluate the business rationale of significant unusual transactions
VSA-053.x:
Basis: VSA 240 (responses to management override).
Analysis: Three mandatory procedures: (A) test the appropriateness of journal entries and FS-preparation adjustments; (B) review accounting estimates for bias (including retrospective review of prior estimates); (C) evaluate the business rationale of significant unusual transactions.
Distractors: (D) Confirming every customer isn't mandated by VSA 240.

VSA-054.q: Match each element of the fraud triangle with an example:
VSA-054.e: VSA 240 requires considering fraud risk factors in risk assessment.
p: Management bonuses tied to hard-to-reach profit targets
One person both records and holds cash, with no reconciliation
Believing it is 'just borrowing and will be repaid'
VSA-054.x:
Basis: VSA 240 (fraud risk factors).
Analysis: Incentive/pressure – management bonuses tied to hard profit targets; opportunity – one person both recording and holding cash with no reconciliation; attitude/rationalisation – 'just borrowing, I'll pay it back'. VSA 240 requires considering these in fraud risk assessment.

VSA-055.q: Under VSA 315, which is NOT part of understanding the entity?
VSA-055.e: Understanding covers industry and regulation; the entity's nature; accounting policies; objectives and strategies; performance measurement; internal control.
o: Internal control relevant to the audit
VSA-055.x:
Basis: VSA 315 (Circular 214/2012/TT-BTC).
Analysis: The auditor understands: industry, regulatory and external factors; the entity's nature (ownership, governance, operations, investing, financing); accounting policies; objectives, strategies and business risks; performance measurement; and relevant internal control.
Distractors: A – shareholders' personal investment plans aren't part of the entity and don't bear on FS misstatement risk.

VSA-056.q: Analytical procedures are mandatory at the risk assessment stage.
VSA-056.e: True (VSA 315), and mandatory at the overall review near the end of the audit (VSA 520).
VSA-056.x:
Basis: VSA 315; VSA 520 (Circular 214/2012/TT-BTC).
Analysis: True. Analytical procedures are mandatory at risk assessment (VSA 315 – spotting unusual movements) and at the overall review near the end (VSA 520 – consistency of the FS with the auditor's understanding). During fieldwork, substantive analytics are optional (VSA-071).

VSA-057.q: Under VSA 330, regardless of assessed risks, the auditor must:
VSA-057.e: This reflects the limitations of risk assessment and internal control.
o: Design and perform substantive procedures for each material class of transactions, account balance and disclosure
VSA-057.x:
Basis: VSA 330 (Circular 214/2012/TT-BTC).
Analysis: Regardless of the risk assessment, the auditor must design and perform substantive procedures for each material class of transactions, account balance and disclosure – since risk assessment is judgmental and IC has inherent limits (override).
Distractors: B, C and D are excessive and not required.

VSA-058.q: If the auditor plans to rely on controls' operating effectiveness to reduce substantive testing, the controls must be tested.
VSA-058.e: True. Untested controls cannot be relied upon.
VSA-058.x:
Basis: VSA 330.
Analysis: True. To assess control risk as low and cut substantive work, the auditor needs evidence of operating effectiveness throughout the reliance period – via tests of controls. A walkthrough shows only design and implementation, which isn't enough (ICR-053).

VSA-059.q: The entity outsources payroll. Under VSA 402, the auditor may use:
VSA-059.e: The auditor must still evaluate the report's adequacy for audit purposes.
o: A type 1 or type 2 report from the service organisation's auditor on its controls
A commitment letter from payroll staff
VSA-059.x:
Basis: VSA 402 – Audit considerations relating to entities using service organisations.
Analysis: The auditor may use the service auditor's Type 1 report (description and design at a point in time) or Type 2 (adding operating effectiveness over a period), after assessing that auditor's competence and independence and the report's fit (period, scope).
Distractors: B and C aren't control evidence; D is wrong as outsourcing doesn't remove risk.

VSA-060.q: To rely on the operating effectiveness of controls at a service organisation to reduce substantive procedures, the auditor needs:
VSA-060.e: A type 1 report only covers design at a point in time, insufficient to rely on operating effectiveness.
o: A type 2 report (design and operating effectiveness of controls over a period)
A type 1 report (design at a point in time)
A management representation letter from the entity
VSA-060.x:
Basis: VSA 402.
Analysis: To rely on service-organisation controls operating effectively, a Type 2 report is needed – covering design and operating effectiveness over a period, with the service auditor's tests. Type 1 shows design only at a point in time – not operation through the period.
Distractors: B isn't enough; C and D aren't evidence about controls at the service organisation.

VSA-061.q: Under VSA 500, audit evidence must be:
VSA-061.e: Higher-quality evidence may need less; but more poor evidence cannot compensate for quality.
VSA-061.x:
Basis: VSA 500 – Audit evidence.
Analysis: Evidence must be sufficient (quantity – driven by risk and quality) and appropriate (quality: relevant to the assertion and reliable). They interact: higher quality may need less, but more poor evidence can't make up for low quality.
Distractors: B looks only at quantity; C and D are wrong.

VSA-062.q: Select ALL factors that increase the reliability of audit evidence:
VSA-062.e: Oral explanations are less reliable than documentary evidence.
VSA-062.x:
Basis: VSA 500.
Analysis: Reliability rises when evidence is: (A) from independent external sources; (B) obtained directly by the auditor (observation, recalculation); (C) documentary (paper or electronic); (D) original rather than copies or faxes; internal evidence is stronger when IC is effective.
Distractors: (E) Oral explanations are least reliable and need corroboration.

VSA-063.q: Match each assertion with a typical audit procedure:
VSA-063.e: Procedures must target assertions at risk.
p: Trace from source documents to the accounting records
Test transactions just before and after period end
VSA-063.x:
Basis: VSA 315; VSA 500.
Analysis: Existence – stock-take attendance, confirmations (assets are real); completeness – tracing from source documents to the books (nothing omitted); valuation – reviewing allowances, NRV (right amount); cut-off – testing transactions either side of year-end. Procedures target the assertions at risk.

VSA-064.q: Vouching from the accounting records back to source documents mainly provides evidence of existence/occurrence.
VSA-064.e: True. The reverse direction (tracing) tests completeness.
VSA-064.x:
Basis: VSA 500.
Analysis: True. Vouching (ledger to documents) checks recorded items are genuine – existence/occurrence, catching overstatement. Tracing (documents to ledger) checks that transactions were recorded – completeness. The direction determines which assertion is tested (VSA-065).

VSA-065.q: Selecting delivery notes and invoices and tracing them to the sales ledger tests the completeness of revenue.
VSA-065.e: True. Transactions that occurred must be recorded.
VSA-065.x:
Basis: VSA 500.
Analysis: True. Starting from evidence that a transaction occurred (delivery notes, invoices) and finding it in the sales ledger → tracing → completeness (understated revenue). Conversely, sampling from the sales ledger to delivery documents tests occurrence (fictitious revenue).

VSA-066.q: Under VSA 501, when inventory is material, the auditor must:
VSA-066.e: If attendance is impracticable, perform alternative procedures; failing that, consider the effect on the opinion.
o: Attend the physical inventory count (unless impracticable)
VSA-066.x:
Basis: VSA 501 – Audit evidence – specific considerations.
Analysis: When inventory is material, the auditor must attend the physical count (unless impracticable) to evaluate instructions, observe procedures, inspect stock and perform test counts. If not possible: alternative procedures; failing that, consider the opinion impact (qualified or disclaimer).
Distractors: B, C and D don't give enough existence evidence.

VSA-067.q: A positive confirmation is one that:
VSA-067.e: A negative confirmation asks for a reply only when there is disagreement.
o: Asks the confirming party to respond in all cases, agreeing or disagreeing
VSA-067.x:
Basis: VSA 505 – External confirmations.
Analysis: Positive confirmations ask the confirming party to reply in all cases – agreeing, disagreeing or supplying figures. No reply means no evidence → alternative procedures (VSA-070).
Distractors: B is a negative confirmation; C – a third party must reply; D – the auditor must control sending and receiving.

VSA-068.q: Negative confirmations are appropriate only when RMM is low, the population has many small homogeneous balances, and expected exceptions are low.
VSA-068.e: True. Negative confirmations should not be the sole substantive procedure for high risks.
VSA-068.x:
Basis: VSA 505.
Analysis: True. Negative confirmations (reply only if disagreeing) give weaker evidence – silence may mean agreement or not reading. They may be the sole substantive procedure only when: RMM is low with controls tested; many small, homogeneous balances; low expected exceptions; and no reason to expect recipients to ignore them.

VSA-069.q: Management refuses to let the auditor confirm a major customer. The auditor should:
VSA-069.e: The refusal may indicate a fraud risk.
o: Inquire about the reasons, evaluate their reasonableness, perform alternative procedures; if unreasonable, communicate with those charged with governance and consider the opinion
VSA-069.x:
Basis: VSA 505 (management refuses a confirmation request).
Analysis: The auditor must: ask why and seek evidence on reasonableness; assess the impact on fraud risk; perform alternative procedures. If the reason is unreasonable or no alternative evidence is obtained: communicate with those charged with governance and consider the opinion (scope limitation).
Distractors: B ignores a red flag; C breaches the agreement and ethics; D is premature.

VSA-070.q: A suitable alternative procedure when a receivable confirmation is not returned:
VSA-070.e: Cash received after period end is strong evidence of receivable existence.
o: Examine subsequent cash receipts and related shipping documents
Obtain an oral confirmation from the AR clerk
VSA-070.x:
Basis: VSA 505 (alternative procedures).
Analysis: Testing post-year-end cash receipts (the customer paid the year-end balance) plus delivery notes, invoices and orders – strong existence evidence, since cash comes from a third party.
Distractors: B offers no evidence; C and D are internal, not independent.
Note: Match receipts to the invoices making up the year-end balance, not later invoices.

VSA-071.q: Under VSA 520, analytical procedures are mandatory:
VSA-071.e: Substantive analytical procedures during fieldwork are at the auditor's choice.
o: Near the end of the audit, when forming an overall conclusion on the FS
VSA-071.x:
Basis: VSA 520 – Analytical procedures.
Analysis: VSA 520 mandates analytical procedures near the end of the audit when forming the overall conclusion – checking the FS are consistent with the auditor's understanding. Substantive analytics (replacing some tests of details) during fieldwork are optional.
Distractors: B, C and D misstate the standard. Analytics are also mandatory at risk assessment under VSA 315 (VSA-056).

VSA-072.q: Average borrowings are VND 200 billion at an average rate of 9% per year. Recorded interest expense is 21 billion. What is the difference between recorded and the auditor's expectation (VND billion)?
VSA-072.e: Expectation = 200 × 9% = 18 billion; difference 21 − 18 = 3 billion, to be investigated if above the threshold.
VSA-072.x:
Basis: VSA 520 (substantive analytics – independent expectation).
Working: Expectation = 200 × 9% = 18 billion. Difference = 21 − 18 = 3 billion VND (16.7% of recorded).
Note: Compare with the acceptable threshold (linked to performance materiality); above it, investigate: prepayment fees, penalty interest, short-term borrowings missing from the average, or interest that should have been capitalised.

VSA-073.e: Using wrong procedures or misinterpreting evidence is non-sampling risk.
o: The risk that the conclusion based on a sample differs from the conclusion if the whole population were tested
The risk of using wrong procedures
VSA-073.x:
Basis: VSA 530 – Audit sampling.
Analysis: Sampling risk is that the conclusion from a sample differs from what testing the whole population would show – either concluding controls are better or errors fewer than reality (affects effectiveness – dangerous), or the reverse (affects efficiency).
Distractors: C is non-sampling risk (VSA-074); B and D are other risks.

VSA-074.q: Non-sampling risk arises when the auditor uses inappropriate procedures or misinterprets evidence; it is reduced by good planning, supervision and review.
VSA-074.e: True. Larger samples do not reduce non-sampling risk.
VSA-074.x:
Basis: VSA 530.
Analysis: True. Non-sampling risk arises from reasons unrelated to sampling: inappropriate procedures, misinterpreting evidence, failing to recognise a deviation. It's reduced by planning, supervision, review and training; larger samples don't help (testing the wrong way more often is still wrong).

VSA-075.q: A sample worth VND 500 million contains 10 million of misstatement; the population is 20 billion. What is the projected misstatement using the ratio method (VND million)?
VSA-075.x:
Basis: VSA 530 (projecting misstatements – ratio method).
Working: Sample error rate = 10 / 500 = 2%. Projected population misstatement = 2% × 20,000 = 400 million VND.
Note: Add an allowance for sampling risk for the upper limit, and compare with tolerable misstatement (often performance materiality). Confirmed anomalies may be excluded from projection.

VSA-076.q: Monetary unit sampling: population VND 10 billion, sample size 50. What is the sampling interval (VND million)?
VSA-076.e: 10,000 / 50 = 200 million VND; items larger than the interval are certain to be selected.
VSA-076.x:
Basis: VSA 530 (monetary unit sampling – MUS).
Working: Interval = 10,000 / 50 = 200 million VND. Pick a random start within the first 200 million, then select the item containing each 200-million cumulative point.
Note: Items ≥ 200 million are certain to be picked; MUS favours large items, so it suits overstatement (existence) testing, less so understatement.

VSA-077.q: Which factor INCREASES sample size in tests of details?
VSA-077.e: The smaller the tolerable misstatement, the larger the sample needed for the same assurance.
o: Lower assessed risk of material misstatement
More other evidence for the same assertion
VSA-077.x:
Basis: VSA 530 (factors affecting sample size for tests of details).
Analysis: Lower tolerable misstatement → more precision needed → larger sample.
Distractors: B goes the other way; C – lower RMM → smaller sample; D – other evidence for the same assertion → smaller sample.
Note: Other drivers of larger samples: higher RMM, larger expected misstatement, higher desired assurance, less homogeneous populations.

VSA-078.q: Which is NOT an approach to testing accounting estimates under VSA 540?
VSA-078.e: Management's experience does not replace audit evidence.
o: Accept the estimate because management is experienced
Test how management made the estimate and the data used
Develop an independent point estimate or range
Consider events up to the date of the auditor's report
VSA-078.x:
Basis: VSA 540 – Auditing accounting estimates.
Analysis: VSA 540 approaches: (B) test management's method, assumptions and data; (C) develop an independent point estimate or range; (D) use events up to the report date (e.g., post-year-end collections); plus testing controls over the estimation process.
Distractors: A – management's experience isn't evidence; accepting it breaches skepticism, especially for bias-prone estimates.

VSA-079.q: Accounting estimates with high estimation uncertainty (e.g., fair value of assets without a market) may be significant risks.
VSA-079.e: True. They require specific responses and possibly experts.
VSA-079.x:
Basis: VSA 540; VSA 315 (significant risks).
Analysis: True. High-uncertainty estimates (fair value of assets without markets, litigation provisions, goodwill impairment) are error- and bias-prone → may be significant risks needing specific responses (VSA-050), testing key assumptions and sensitivity, and possibly experts (VSA 620).

VSA-080.q: Under VSA 550, the auditor pays particular attention to:
VSA-080.e: Unusual related-party transactions carry high risks of fraud and inadequate disclosure.
o: Significant related-party transactions outside the normal course of business
VSA-080.x:
Basis: VSA 550 – Related parties.
Analysis: Auditors focus on significant related-party transactions outside the normal course of business – high fraud risk (shifting value, hiding obligations) and disclosure risk; contracts, business rationale, approvals and disclosures must be examined.
Distractors: B and C are routine, low-risk; D – an unrelated bank isn't a related party.

VSA-081.q: Match each event with its treatment under VSA 560 and accounting standards:
VSA-081.e: Events providing evidence of conditions existing at period end are adjusting events.
p: A court ruling after period end confirms an obligation existing at period end
A warehouse fire after period end
Do not adjust; disclose if material
The auditor learns of a material fact after the report is issued
Discuss with management; consider amending the FS and the report
VSA-081.x:
Basis: VSA 560; VAS 23.
Analysis: A court ruling confirming an obligation existing at year-end → adjusting event (evidence of a condition that existed); a warehouse fire after year-end → a new event, non-adjusting, disclosed if material; a material fact learned after the report is issued → discuss with management, consider amending the FS and the report (VSA-134).

VSA-082.q: After the report is issued, the auditor has no obligation to perform further procedures, but if a fact that might change the report becomes known, it must be considered.
VSA-082.x:
Basis: VSA 560.
Analysis: True. After the report is issued, the auditor has no duty to perform further procedures on the FS. But if they learn a fact that, known at the report date, might have changed the report, they must discuss with management, decide whether the FS need amending and respond appropriately.

VSA-083.q: Under VSA 570, the minimum period of management's going concern assessment the auditor considers is:
VSA-083.e: If management's assessment covers less, the auditor asks to extend it.
o: 12 months from the end of the reporting period
VSA-083.x:
Basis: VSA 570 – Going concern.
Analysis: The auditor evaluates management's assessment over the period management used under the framework; if under 12 months from the period end, the auditor asks management to extend it to at least 12 months.
Distractors: B, C and D aren't the standard's period.

VSA-084.q: Select ALL indicators that may cast doubt on going concern:
VSA-084.e: Steady profit growth is not a going concern risk indicator.
o: Large operating losses, negative operating cash flow
Loss of a major customer or supplier
VSA-084.x:
Basis: VSA 570 (events or conditions casting doubt on going concern).
Analysis: Indicators: (A) current liabilities > current assets – negative working capital; (B) heavy losses, negative operating cash flow; (C) inability to pay debts as due, covenant breaches; (D) loss of a key customer or supplier (ICR-160).
Distractors: (E) Steady multi-year profit growth is a positive sign.

VSA-085.q: Under VSA 580, the written representation letter must be dated:
VSA-085.e: Representations must cover all FS and periods reported on.
o: As near as practicable to, but not after, the date of the auditor's report
30 days after the report is issued
VSA-085.x:
Basis: VSA 580 – Written representations.
Analysis: The letter should be dated as near as practicable to, but not after, the audit report date – so it covers events up to the report. It must cover all FS and periods reported on.
Distractors: B is too early to cover subsequent events; C is pointless after issue; D is wrong.

VSA-086.q: Written representations are necessary audit evidence but do not replace other evidence the auditor must obtain.
VSA-086.e: True. Representations supplement but do not suffice on their own.
VSA-086.x:
Basis: VSA 580; VSA 500.
Analysis: True. Written representations are necessary evidence (management confirming responsibilities, complete information, all transactions recorded) but internal and never sufficient alone for any assertion. If they conflict with other evidence, the auditor reassesses their reliability and management's integrity.

VSA-087.q: Under VSA 230, assembly of the final audit file is usually completed within:
VSA-087.e: Afterwards, audit documentation may not be deleted or discarded.
o: 60 days after the date of the auditor's report
VSA-087.x:
Basis: VSA 230 (assembling the final audit file).
Analysis: Firms set a deadline to assemble the final file, usually no more than 60 days after the report date. Thereafter documentation may not be deleted or discarded before the retention period ends; additions must be logged (VSA-089).
Distractors: 30 days, 90 days and 12 months are wrong.

VSA-088.q: Audit files must be retained for at least 10 years from the date of the auditor's report.
VSA-088.e: True under the independent audit law.
VSA-088.x:
Basis: Independent Audit Law 67/2011/QH12; VSA 230.
Analysis: True. Audit files are kept for at least 10 years from the report date – for quality inspections, disputes and authorities' requests.
Note: It mirrors the retention period for posting vouchers (10 years – ACC-001).

VSA-089.q: After file completion, if documentation must be added, the auditor records the reasons, timing, preparer and reviewer of the addition.
VSA-089.e: True. Old documents may not be altered; additions must be recorded.
VSA-089.x:
Basis: VSA 230.
Analysis: True. After file assembly, any change or addition must record the specific reasons, when, by whom and who reviewed it; existing documentation can't be altered or deleted – preserving file integrity for inspections.

VSA-090.q: When using internal audit's work under VSA 610, the external auditor:
VSA-090.e: The auditor evaluates internal audit's objectivity, competence and systematic approach.
o: Retains sole responsibility for the audit opinion
Names internal audit in the report
Need not evaluate internal audit's competence
VSA-090.x:
Basis: VSA 610 – Using the work of internal auditors.
Analysis: The external auditor retains sole responsibility for the opinion; it isn't reduced by using IA's work. Before relying, they evaluate IA's objectivity, competence and systematic, disciplined approach, and reperform some of the work.
Distractors: B and C have no basis; D breaches the standard.

VSA-091.q: The auditor uses an expert to value the client's investment property. Under VSA 620, the auditor must:
VSA-091.e: The expert is mentioned in the report only when required by law or relevant to a modified opinion.
o: Evaluate the expert's competence, capabilities, objectivity and the adequacy of the work
Name the expert to share responsibility
Not agree the scope of work
VSA-091.x:
Basis: VSA 620 – Using the work of an auditor's expert.
Analysis: The auditor must: evaluate the expert's competence, capabilities and objectivity; understand their field; agree scope and objectives; and evaluate the adequacy of the work (assumptions, methods, source data).
Distractors: B breaches skepticism; C – the auditor doesn't share responsibility; D breaches the standard.
Note: Mention the expert in the report only if law requires or it relates to a modified opinion.

VSA-092.q: Match each situation with the type of audit opinion:
p: FS present fairly in all material respects
Unable to obtain evidence; possible effects material and pervasive
VSA-092.x:
Basis: VSA 700; VSA 705.
Analysis: Opinion matrix: true and fair in all material respects → unmodified; material but not pervasive misstatement → qualified; material and pervasive misstatement → adverse; unable to obtain evidence with possibly material and pervasive effects → disclaimer. A material but not pervasive scope limitation → qualified.

VSA-093.q: An adverse opinion is issued when:
VSA-093.e: An adverse opinion is the most severe opinion on misstatement.
o: The FS contain material and pervasive misstatement
Evidence cannot be obtained for a minor item
There is an emphasis of matter paragraph
The entity changed accounting policy with full disclosure
VSA-093.x:
Basis: VSA 705.
Analysis: An adverse opinion is given when, having obtained sufficient evidence, the auditor concludes misstatements, individually or combined, are material and pervasive.
Distractors: B – an immaterial item doesn't modify the opinion; C – emphasis of matter doesn't change it (VSA-097); D – a properly disclosed policy change isn't a misstatement.

VSA-094.q: A disclaimer of opinion is issued when:
VSA-094.e: Unlike an adverse opinion (misstatement identified), a disclaimer stems from scope limitation.
o: The auditor cannot obtain sufficient appropriate evidence and possible effects are material and pervasive
Management agrees to correct all misstatements
VSA-094.x:
Basis: VSA 705.
Analysis: A disclaimer is given when the auditor can't obtain sufficient appropriate evidence and concludes the possible effects of undetected misstatements are material and pervasive. Unlike adverse (misstatement identified), a disclaimer stems from a scope limitation.
Distractors: B, C and D don't reach that level.

VSA-095.q: 'Pervasive' effects are not confined to specific items, or represent a substantial proportion of the FS, or relate to disclosures fundamental to users' understanding.
VSA-095.x:
Basis: VSA 705 (definition of 'pervasive').
Analysis: True. Effects are pervasive if, in the auditor's judgment, they: (1) aren't confined to specific items or accounts; or (2) if confined, represent a substantial part of the FS; or (3) for disclosures, are fundamental to users' understanding. Example in VSA-129: inventory at 60% of total assets.

VSA-096.q: An 'Emphasis of matter' paragraph (VSA 706) is used to:
VSA-096.e: It does not modify the audit opinion.
o: Draw users' attention to a matter presented or disclosed in the FS that is fundamental to their understanding
VSA-096.x:
Basis: VSA 706 – Emphasis of Matter and Other Matter paragraphs.
Analysis: An Emphasis of Matter paragraph draws attention to a matter properly presented or disclosed in the FS that the auditor considers fundamental to users' understanding (e.g., litigation uncertainty, a major catastrophe).
Distractors: B and C – emphasis doesn't replace a modified opinion; D – it isn't a disclaimer of responsibility.

VSA-097.q: An emphasis of matter paragraph turns the opinion into a qualified opinion.
VSA-097.e: False. The opinion is unchanged; the paragraph only draws attention.
VSA-097.x:
Basis: VSA 706.
Analysis: False. An Emphasis of Matter paragraph doesn't modify the opinion – it stays unmodified (or whatever was given); it merely directs readers to a disclosed matter.

VSA-098.q: An 'Other matter' paragraph is used for:
VSA-098.e: E.g., the prior-year FS were audited by another auditor.
o: Matters not presented in the FS but relevant to understanding the audit, the auditor's responsibilities or the report
Matters already disclosed in the FS
VSA-098.x:
Basis: VSA 706.
Analysis: An Other Matter paragraph covers matters not presented in the FS but relevant to understanding the audit, the auditor's responsibilities or the report – e.g., prior-year FS audited by another auditor, restrictions on distribution.
Distractors: B uses Emphasis of Matter; C and D lead to modified opinions (VSA 705).

VSA-099.q: When a material uncertainty about going concern exists and is adequately disclosed, the auditor issues an unmodified opinion with a paragraph drawing attention to it.
VSA-099.e: True. If disclosure is inadequate, the opinion is qualified or adverse.
VSA-099.x:
Basis: VSA 570; VSA 706.
Analysis: True. A material going-concern uncertainty, with the assumption still appropriate and adequately disclosed → unmodified opinion with a paragraph drawing attention to it. Inadequate disclosure → qualified or adverse depending on severity. An inappropriate assumption → adverse (VSA-100).

VSA-100.q: The auditor concludes the going concern basis is inappropriate, but the FS are still prepared on that basis. The opinion is:
VSA-100.e: Using an inappropriate basis pervasively affects the whole FS.
VSA-100.x:
Basis: VSA 570.
Analysis: If the auditor concludes the going-concern basis is inappropriate but the FS still use it, the whole measurement basis (historical cost, current/non-current classification) is wrong → pervasive → adverse opinion, even with disclosure.
Distractors: B is for a disclosed material uncertainty; C is a scope limitation; D is wrong.

VSA-101.q: Key audit matters (KAM) under ISA 701/draft VSA 701 are:
VSA-101.e: KAM are mandatory for listed entities and show users the audit's focus.
o: Matters of most significance in the current-period audit in the auditor's judgement, selected from matters communicated with those charged with governance
VSA-101.x:
Basis: ISA 701; draft VSA 701 (2026) (per the question's source).
Analysis: KAMs are the matters of most significance in the auditor's judgment in the current audit, selected from those communicated with governance (high risk, significant judgments, major events). Mandatory for listed entities.
Distractors: B and C aren't KAMs; D – a qualified opinion is a modification, not a KAM (VSA-102).

VSA-102.q: Presenting a key audit matter can substitute for a qualified opinion.
VSA-102.e: False. KAM do not replace a modified opinion; matters giving rise to a modification are not presented as KAM.
VSA-102.x:
Basis: ISA 701; draft VSA 701 (2026).
Analysis: False. KAMs don't substitute for a modified opinion required by VSA 705; matters causing a qualified or adverse opinion go in the 'Basis for opinion' section, not as KAMs. KAMs only describe the audit's focus and how it was addressed.

VSA-103.q: Under VSA 720, regarding other information in the annual report, the auditor:
VSA-103.e: If inconsistencies are found, the auditor determines whether the FS or the other information needs revision.
o: Reads it to identify material inconsistencies with the audited FS
Audits it and expresses an opinion
VSA-103.x:
Basis: VSA 720 – The auditor's responsibilities relating to other information.
Analysis: The auditor reads other information (annual report, management report) and considers whether it is materially inconsistent with the audited FS or the auditor's knowledge; if so, decides whether the FS or the other information needs amending.
Distractors: B – the auditor doesn't audit it; C is wrong as reading is required; D isn't required.

VSA-104.e: Initial engagements – opening balances is VSA 510.
o: Comparative information – corresponding figures and comparative FS
VSA-104.x:
Basis: VSA 710 – Comparative information.
Analysis: VSA 710 covers the auditor's duties on comparatives: corresponding figures (prior-period amounts as part of current FS) and comparative FS (prior FS presented and covered by the opinion).
Distractors: B – initial audits and opening balances are VSA 510; C – VSA 720; D – VSA 810.

VSA-105.q: Consider these statements on the auditor's report:
VSA-105.e: The report may not be dated before the FS are prepared and those with authority take responsibility for them.
o: The report must be signed by a practising auditor.
The report date may precede management's approval of the FS.
The report must state the audit firm's name and address.
VSA-105.x:
Basis: VSA 700 – Forming an opinion and reporting on FS.
Analysis: True: the report must be dated; signed by the practising auditor (and the firm's representative); and show the firm's name and address. False: the report can't be dated before the FS are prepared and those with authority acknowledge responsibility (VSA-106).

VSA-106.q: The auditor's report may not be dated before sufficient appropriate evidence is obtained, including evidence that the FS have been prepared and those with authority have accepted responsibility.
VSA-106.x:
Basis: VSA 700.
Analysis: True. The report can't be dated before sufficient appropriate evidence is obtained, including that the complete FS (with notes) have been prepared and those with authority have taken responsibility. The report date also bounds the auditor's duties for subsequent events (VSA 560).

VSA-107.q: Before signing, management imposes a scope limitation that the auditor believes will lead to a disclaimer. The auditor should:
VSA-107.e: Under VSA 210, such a limitation removes the preconditions for an audit.
o: Not accept the engagement (unless required by law)
Accept and issue an unmodified opinion
VSA-107.x:
Basis: VSA 210; VSA 705.
Analysis: If management imposes a pre-engagement scope limitation the auditor expects to cause a disclaimer, the auditor shouldn't accept the engagement (unless required by law) – the audit's preconditions aren't met.
Distractors: B and C breach the standards; D – a higher fee doesn't remove the limitation.

VSA-108.q: Under VSA 265, significant deficiencies in internal control must be communicated:
o: In writing, on a timely basis, to those charged with governance (and management at the appropriate level)
VSA-108.x:
Basis: VSA 265 – Communicating deficiencies in internal control.
Analysis: Significant deficiencies must be communicated in writing, timely, to those charged with governance, and to management at an appropriate level (unless inappropriate, e.g., involving management fraud). Usually via a management letter.
Distractors: B and C aren't enough; D – the FS audit report doesn't list control deficiencies.

VSA-109.q: Under VSA 260, the auditor communicates with those charged with governance about planned scope, timing and significant findings.
VSA-109.e: True. Two-way communication supports governance oversight.
VSA-109.x:
Basis: VSA 260 – Communication with those charged with governance.
Analysis: True. The auditor communicates: their responsibilities; planned scope and timing (significant risks); significant findings (accounting practices, difficulties, uncorrected misstatements); independence (for listed entities). Two-way communication helps governance oversight and gives the auditor information.

VSA-110.q: Under VSA 450, the auditor accumulates misstatements identified during the audit, except:
VSA-110.e: Corrected misstatements are still accumulated and communicated.
VSA-110.x:
Basis: VSA 450.
Analysis: The auditor accumulates all identified misstatements except those clearly trivial (below the threshold – VSA-047).
Distractors: B – fraud-related misstatements always need qualitative review, however small; C – disclosure misstatements are accumulated too; D – corrected misstatements are still accumulated and communicated.

VSA-111.q: Uncorrected misstatements: revenue cut-off 300 million, under-provision 450 million, unrecorded expenses 200 million (all overstating profit). What is the total uncorrected misstatement (VND million)?
VSA-111.x:
Basis: VSA 450.
Working: Total uncorrected misstatements (all increasing profit) = 300 + 450 + 200 = 950 million VND.
Note: Opposite-direction errors may offset in the profit effect, but each must still be assessed individually and for its effect on other line items (assets, classification).

VSA-112.q: Uncorrected misstatements: revenue cut-off 300 million, under-provision 450 million, unrecorded expenses 200 million (all overstating profit, total 950 million). Overall materiality is VND 1,000 million with no special qualitative factors. The most appropriate conclusion:
VSA-112.e: When the total approaches materiality, the risk that undetected misstatements push it over is significant; the auditor may request corrections or extend procedures.
o: Below materiality, so an unmodified opinion is possible, but the risk of undetected misstatement must be considered as the total is close to materiality
VSA-112.x:
Basis: VSA 450; VSA 320.
Analysis: 950 million < 1,000 million materiality with no qualitative factors → quantitatively not material; an unmodified opinion is possible. But at 95% of materiality, the risk that undetected errors push it over is significant → the auditor should request correction or extend procedures.
Distractors: B, C and D overreact when the total is still below materiality.

VSA-113.q: An inventory misstatement of VND 1.5 billion (materiality 1 billion, affecting only inventory and cost of sales) is not corrected. The opinion is:
VSA-113.x:
Basis: VSA 705.
Analysis: A 1.5-billion error > 1-billion materiality → material; it affects only inventory and COGS, not most of the FS → not pervasive; management refuses to correct → qualified opinion.
Distractors: B is for material and pervasive; C for pervasive scope limits; D is wrong given an uncorrected material error.

VSA-114.e: The report should alert users to the special purpose and restrict use.
o: FS prepared under a special purpose framework (e.g., tax basis, contractual provisions)
VSA-114.x:
Basis: VSA 800 – Audits of FS prepared under special purpose frameworks.
Analysis: It applies to FS under special-purpose frameworks (tax basis, cash basis, contract terms, regulatory requirements). The report must describe the purpose, alert readers that the FS may not suit other purposes, and may restrict distribution.
Distractors: B – VSA 600; C – VSA 810; D – a different assurance standard.

VSA-115.e: E.g., auditing revenue alone to compute royalties.
o: Single financial statements or specific elements, accounts or items of FS
VSA-115.x:
Basis: VSA 805 – Audits of single FS and specific elements, accounts or items.
Analysis: VSA 805 covers auditing a single statement (e.g., balance sheet only) or a specific element, account or item (e.g., revenue for royalty calculations, receivables). Materiality is set for that element.
Distractors: B – VSA 700; C – internal control assurance; D – other assurance standards.

VSA-116.e: Summary FS are derived from audited FS.
o: Engagements to report on summary FS
VSA-116.x:
Basis: VSA 810 – Engagements to report on summary FS.
Analysis: VSA 810 covers reporting on summary FS derived from FS the same auditor audited; the auditor opines on whether the summary is consistent in all material respects with the audited FS under the applied criteria.
Distractors: B – VSA 600; C – VSRE 2410; D – VSRS 4400.

VSA-117.q: Match each engagement type with its level of assurance:
VSA-117.e: The assurance level determines the scope of procedures and the form of report.
p: No assurance – report of factual findings only
VSA-117.x:
Basis: Auditing and related services standards (VSA 200; VSRE 2410; VSRS 4400).
Analysis: FS audit – reasonable assurance, positive opinion ('the FS present fairly…'); interim review – limited assurance, negative conclusion ('nothing has come to our attention…'); agreed-upon procedures – no assurance, only factual findings for users to judge.

VSA-118.q: Reviews of half-year FS mainly use inquiry and analytical procedures; the conclusion is negative-form ('nothing has come to our attention...').
VSA-118.e: True. The scope is much narrower than an audit.
VSA-118.x:
Basis: VSRE 2410 – Review of interim financial information by the entity's auditor.
Analysis: True. Reviews rely mainly on inquiry and analytics, without tests of details, stock-take attendance or confirmations as in an audit; hence only a negative-form conclusion with limited assurance.

VSA-119.q: Corporate internal audit under Decree 05/2019/ND-CP is not required to apply the VSAs designed for independent audit.
VSA-119.e: True. Internal audit refers to Decree 05/2019 and IIA standards.
VSA-119.x:
Basis: Decree 05/2019/ND-CP; IIA GIAS 2024.
Analysis: True. VSAs govern independent audits by audit firms. Corporate IA follows Decree 05/2019 (principles, standards, charter) and references international IA standards (IIA GIAS); it may borrow VSA methods (sampling, evidence) but isn't bound by them.

VSA-120.q: To sign an auditor's report, an auditor must have:
VSA-120.e: Only registered practising auditors may sign audit reports.
o: An auditor certificate and a valid audit practice registration certificate
Merely employment at an audit firm
VSA-120.x:
Basis: Independent Audit Law 67/2011/QH12 (practising auditors).
Analysis: To sign an audit report, an auditor needs an auditor certificate (Ministry-issued or a recognised foreign one) and a valid practising registration at an audit firm.
Distractors: B and C don't meet practising conditions; D – an accounting practice certificate doesn't allow signing audit reports.

VSA-121.q: The audited entity is responsible for providing complete, timely documents and information to the auditor.
VSA-121.e: True under the Independent Audit Law; obstruction may cause a scope limitation.
VSA-121.x:
Basis: Independent Audit Law 67/2011/QH12 (rights and duties of audited entities).
Analysis: True. Audited entities must provide complete, timely and truthful documents and information and are responsible for their accuracy. Obstruction may cause a scope limitation → qualified opinion or disclaimer (VSA-094).

VSA-122.q: An audit team member may also serve as the client's chief accountant if the client's management agrees.
VSA-122.e: False. This destroys independence and no safeguard can address it.
VSA-122.x:
Basis: Circular 70/2015/TT-BTC; Independent Audit Law 67/2011/QH12 (cases barring an audit).
Analysis: False. A team member serving as the client's chief accountant takes part in management and prepares the FS being audited – severe self-review and self-interest threats with no safeguard; client consent changes nothing.

VSA-123.q: In a group audit (VSA 600), the group engagement team:
VSA-123.e: The group team decides its involvement in component auditors' work.
o: Directs and supervises the group audit and evaluates the component auditors' work
Only consolidates figures, with no responsibility
Shares responsibility for the opinion with component auditors
Need not communicate with component auditors
VSA-123.x:
Basis: VSA 600 – Group audits.
Analysis: The group engagement team directs, supervises and performs the group audit; understands component auditors (ethics, competence); sets component materiality; decides its involvement and evaluates component auditors' work; and communicates both ways.
Distractors: B and C are wrong – the group report doesn't divide responsibility with component auditors (unless law requires); D breaches the standard.

VSA-124.q: Profit is volatile and near break-even; the auditor uses 0.5% of revenue of VND 800 billion as overall materiality. What is materiality (VND million)?
VSA-124.x:
Basis: VSA 320.
Working: Materiality = 800,000 million × 0.5% = 4,000 million VND.
Note: Near break-even, PBT gives an unrealistically small materiality, so revenue (typically 0.5–1%) or multi-year average profit is used (VSA-044).

VSA-125.q: An investment fund uses 1% of total assets of VND 500 billion as overall materiality. What is materiality (VND billion)?
VSA-125.x:
Basis: VSA 320.
Working: Materiality = 500 × 1% = 5 billion VND.
Note: For investment funds, users focus on net asset value, so total assets or NAV suits better than profit (which swings with markets).

VSA-126.q: During the count, the auditor finds many damaged and expired lots with no provision. The assertion mainly affected is:
VSA-126.e: Damaged goods must be written down to net realisable value.
VSA-126.x:
Basis: VSA 501; VAS 02.
Analysis: Damaged or expired goods still exist and are owned, but their NRV is below cost with no allowance → the valuation assertion is affected: write down to NRV (ACC-090).
Distractors: B – the goods exist; C – nothing was omitted; D – ownership isn't affected.

VSA-127.q: December revenue spikes; early January shows many credit notes and returns. The most appropriate procedure:
VSA-127.e: A classic sign of fictitious or wrongly timed revenue.
o: Test revenue cut-off, post-year-end returns and adjustments; consider revenue fraud risk
VSA-127.x:
Basis: VSA 240; VSA 560; VSA 330.
Analysis: A December revenue spike followed by early-January credit notes and returns is a classic sign of fictitious or mis-dated revenue (channel stuffing). Procedures: cut-off testing around year-end; post-period returns and credit notes; contract terms (return rights); assessing revenue fraud risk (VSA-051).
Distractors: B isn't enough – customers may confirm balances while revenue is still mis-dated; C ignores the red flag; D is unrelated.

VSA-128.q: Appointed after period end, the auditor could not attend the count or perform alternative procedures; inventory is material but effects are not pervasive. The opinion is:
VSA-128.e: Material but not pervasive scope limitation → qualified.
VSA-128.x:
Basis: VSA 501; VSA 705.
Analysis: No stock-take attendance and no possible alternatives → insufficient evidence on inventory (scope limitation). Possible effects are material but not pervasive → qualified opinion for scope limitation.
Distractors: B is for identified, pervasive misstatements; C is wrong given missing material evidence; D applies when pervasive (VSA-129).

VSA-129.q: Same situation, but inventory is 60% of total assets and affects cost of sales, profit, tax and many disclosures. The appropriate opinion:
VSA-129.e: A scope limitation with possibly material and pervasive effects → disclaimer.
VSA-129.x:
Basis: VSA 705.
Analysis: Inventory at 60% of total assets, affecting COGS, profit, tax and many notes → possible effects are material and pervasive (VSA-095); since it's a scope limitation (no evidence), not an identified misstatement → disclaimer of opinion.
Distractors: B applies if not pervasive; C if a misstatement is identified; D doesn't fit.

VSA-130.q: Uncorrected misstatement: fictitious revenue of VND 1.2 billion with related cost of sales of 0.4 billion. By how much is profit before tax overstated (VND million)?
VSA-130.x:
Basis: VSA 450.
Working: Fictitious revenue adds 1,200 million; the matching COGS of 400 million reduces profit → net PBT overstatement = 1,200 − 400 = 800 million VND.
Note: Beyond profit, assess the misstatement in revenue (1.2 billion), receivables and inventory, and its fraudulent nature – intentional misstatements may be qualitatively material even below materiality.

VSA-131.q: 40 items are tested with total misstatement of VND 2 million (average 50,000 per item); the population has 3,000 items. What is projected misstatement using the mean-per-unit method (VND million)?
VSA-131.x:
Basis: VSA 530 (projection – mean-per-unit method).
Working: Average error = 2,000,000 / 40 = 50,000 VND per item. Projected population error = 50,000 × 3,000 = 150,000,000 VND = 150 million VND.
Note: The mean-per-item method suits errors unrelated to item size; the ratio method (VSA-075) suits errors proportional to value.

VSA-132.q: The auditor finds the CFO is a family member of the owner of a major supplier. Transactions with this supplier should be considered related-party transactions.
VSA-132.e: True (VSA 550). Prices, terms and disclosures must be assessed.
VSA-132.x:
Basis: VSA 550; VAS 26.
Analysis: True. The CFO is key management personnel; a close family member owning the supplier makes it a related party under VAS 26. Assess pricing versus market, terms, approval (whether the conflicted person took part) and full disclosure.

VSA-133.q: A listed client asks the audit firm to also keep its books and prepare its FS. The correct assessment:
VSA-133.e: Accounting services for public-interest audit clients are prohibited.
o: Self-review threat; for public interest entities, bookkeeping and FS preparation for audit clients are prohibited
VSA-133.x:
Basis: Circular 70/2015/TT-BTC (non-assurance services to public-interest audit clients); Independent Audit Law 67/2011/QH12.
Analysis: Keeping books and preparing FS then auditing them → self-review threat (VSA-022). For public-interest (listed) entities, the audit firm may not provide bookkeeping or FS preparation to audit clients – no safeguard substitutes.
Distractors: B, C and D are wrong – a separate contract or higher fee doesn't remove the threat.

VSA-134.q: After the report is issued, the auditor learns of a material liability existing at period end that was not recognised. The auditor should:
VSA-134.e: If management refuses, the auditor takes action to prevent reliance on the report.
o: Discuss with management, ask for the FS to be amended and issue a new report on the amended FS
Ignore it since the report is issued
Announce it in the press immediately
VSA-134.x:
Basis: VSA 560 (facts discovered after the report is issued).
Analysis: The auditor discusses with management (and governance) whether the FS need amending; if amended → performs necessary procedures on the changes and issues a new report on the amended FS. If management refuses → acts to prevent reliance on the old report.
Distractors: B ignores the duty; C – the auditor doesn't adjust the client's books; D breaches confidentiality.

VSA-135.q: Arrange the phases of a financial statement audit:
VSA-135.e: Each phase must be documented in the file.
o: Accept the client and sign the engagement letter
Perform tests of controls and substantive procedures
Complete: evaluate misstatements, subsequent events, going concern, representations
Issue the auditor's report and management letter
VSA-135.x:
Basis: VSA set (VSA 210, 300, 315, 330, 450, 560, 570, 580, 700).
Analysis: Order: client acceptance and engagement (VSA 210) → planning and risk assessment (VSA 300, 315, 320) → tests of controls and substantive procedures (VSA 330, 500) → completion: misstatements, subsequent events, going concern, representations (VSA 450, 560, 570, 580) → report and management letter (VSA 700, 265). Each stage is documented (VSA 230).

VSA-136.q: Auditing inventory of a multi-branch supermarket chain. Select ALL appropriate procedures:
VSA-136.e: Accepting figures untested breaches the sufficient appropriate evidence requirement.
o: Attend counts at significant branches with two-way test counts (records → floor, floor → records)
Test expired and slow-moving goods and the write-down provision
Use internal audit's or an expert's work when needed, after evaluation
VSA-136.x:
Basis: VSA 500; VSA 501; VSA 610; VSA 620; VAS 02.
Analysis: Suitable procedures: (A) attend counts at significant branches with two-way test counts – book to floor (existence), floor to book (completeness); (B) check expired and slow-moving stock and allowances (valuation); (C) use IA or experts after assessing competence and objectivity.
Distractors: (D) Accepting untested figures breaches the sufficient, appropriate evidence requirement.

VSA-137.q: Testing payment approval controls: of 60 payment vouchers, 3 lack approval. What is the sample deviation rate (%)?
VSA-137.x:
Basis: VSA 530.
Working: Sample deviation rate = 3 / 60 = 5%.
Note: The conclusion compares this with the tolerable rate, allowing for sampling risk (VSA-138).

VSA-138.q: Test of payment approval control: 60 vouchers tested, 3 lacked approval (sample deviation rate 5%). Tolerable deviation is 5%, expected 3%. The appropriate conclusion:
VSA-138.e: The sample rate already equals tolerable; with sampling risk the population rate may exceed it.
o: Do not rely on this control; extend substantive testing of expenses
The control is effective; reduce substantive work
VSA-138.x:
Basis: VSA 330; VSA 530.
Analysis: A 5% sample rate already equals the 5% tolerable rate and exceeds the 3% expected; with sampling risk the population upper limit exceeds 5% → the control can't be relied on; extend substantive testing of expenses and report the deficiency.
Distractors: B reverses the conclusion; C ignores the statistics; D is premature – a control deficiency doesn't automatically mean a qualified opinion.

VSA-139.q: The chief accountant's oral confirmation of bank balances is sufficient to replace a bank confirmation.
VSA-139.e: False. Internal oral evidence is less reliable than direct confirmation from the bank.
VSA-139.x:
Basis: VSA 500; VSA 505.
Analysis: False. A chief accountant's oral statement is internal and oral – the least reliable evidence (VSA-062). A bank confirmation sent directly to the auditor is independent, external and written, and also reveals loans, guarantees and pledges.

VSA-140.q: The auditor finds indications of fraud by a warehouse employee, immaterial in amount. The auditor should:
VSA-140.e: VSA 240 requires communicating fraud even when immaterial; consider legal reporting duties.
o: Communicate promptly with the appropriate level of management; if management or key staff are involved, with those charged with governance
VSA-140.x:
Basis: VSA 240 (communicating fraud).
Analysis: On identifying or learning of fraud, the auditor communicates promptly with the appropriate level of management – even if immaterial; if it involves management, key employees or causes material misstatement, with those charged with governance; and considers any legal duty to report to authorities.
Distractors: B – small frauds may signal bigger control failures; C – it isn't the first step and depends on law; D – the auditor can't discipline client staff.
